title: Git Internals
summary: Git as a content-addressed database of blobs, trees and commits; branches as pointers; what merge and rebase really do; and why the same ideas power caches and replicas.

questions.prompt: What *is* a Git branch, physically? Why is creating one instant even in a huge repository?
keyPoints: A branch is a small file (a ref) containing one commit hash
HEAD normally points to the current branch name, which points to a commit
Creating a branch writes one tiny file; no files or commits are copied
Committing creates a new commit and moves the current branch pointer to it

questions.prompt: Describe Git's object model: what are blobs, trees and commits, and how are they named? Why does changing one byte in a commit from last year change the hash of every commit after it?
questions.hint: What does each object's hash cover?
keyPoints: Objects are content-addressed: named by the SHA-1 hash of their type, size and content
Blob = file contents; tree = directory listing mapping names to blob/tree hashes; commit = root tree hash, parent hash(es), author, committer, message
A commit's hash covers its tree and its parent's hash, so it transitively covers all history (a Merkle structure)
Changing an old commit changes its hash, which changes its child's parent field and therefore the child's hash, and so on
This gives integrity checking and deduplication of unchanged files across snapshots

questions.prompt: Write a Node.js function `gitBlobHash(content)` that returns the same hash as `git hash-object` for a UTF-8 string. Then explain why `gitBlobHash('héllo\n')` must use the **byte** length, not `content.length`.
questions.hint: Git hashes a header `blob <size>\0` followed by the bytes. Remember Day 3: UTF-8 characters can be more than one byte.
keyPoints: Build the header `blob <byteLength>\0` and hash header + content bytes with SHA-1
Return the hex digest (40 hex characters)
Use `Buffer.byteLength` or `Buffer.from(content).length`, not `content.length`
`é` is 2 bytes in UTF-8 but 1 UTF-16 code unit in JS, so `content.length` would give the wrong size and the wrong hash

questions.prompt: A teammate rebased the shared `develop` branch onto `main` and force-pushed. Now everyone's pulls show conflicts and duplicate-looking commits. Explain what happened, and how you'd fix it and prevent it.
questions.hint: Does rebase move commits or create new ones?
keyPoints: Rebase replays commits onto a new base, creating new commits with new hashes (different parents)
Teammates still have the old commits; Git sees old and new as different work, causing duplicates and conflicts when they pull or merge
Fix: teammates rebase their local work onto the new develop (or reset to it after saving their own commits), or the original commits can be restored using the reflog and force-pushed back
Prevention: don't rebase shared or published branches; use merge there; protect shared branches against force-push

questions.prompt: A giant monorepo holds **10 billion** Git objects. Using the birthday approximation `P ≈ n² / 2^161`, estimate the probability that two *different* objects accidentally share a SHA-1 hash. Should the team worry? What's the real risk?
keyPoints: Accidental collisions are effectively impossible
The real risk is deliberate collisions, since practical SHA-1 collisions were demonstrated (SHAttered, 2017); Git added collision detection and supports SHA-256
questions.answer: `P ≈ (10^10)² / 2^161 = 10^20 / 2.9×10^48 ≈ 3.4 × 10^-29`. Accidental collision: no worry. Deliberate attacks are the concern, mitigated by Git's hardened SHA-1 collision detection and the SHA-256 object format.

questions.prompt: Using ideas from Git, sketch how a file-sync service (like Dropbox) could detect which files changed between a laptop with **200,000 files** and the server, while sending as little data as possible.
questions.hint: Hash files, then hash directories of hashes. Compare from the top down.
keyPoints: Hash each file's contents (or fixed-size chunks of each file) to get content addresses
Build a Merkle tree: each directory's hash covers the hashes of its children, up to one root hash
Compare root hashes first; if equal, nothing changed. Otherwise descend only into subtrees whose hashes differ
Work is proportional to the number of changed paths times tree depth, not to all 200,000 files
Upload only chunks the server doesn't already have (content-addressed dedup), which also saves space for duplicate files across users
